claim: On average the VIX over-forecasts the next month's variance: the mean scaled seller payoff is 24.2% of implied variance (95% CI 12.0% to 36.5%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / mean: 0.2423 [0.1198, 0.3648] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 3.88, p = 0.000106; payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / mean: 0.2423 [0.1137, 0.3563] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = 0.0005

claim: The raw variance payoff is positive on average: 0.007642 in annualised variance (95% CI -8.458e-04 to 0.01613).
reasons: payoff_var: CI [-8.458e-04, 0.01613] does not exclude 0; payoff_var: CI [-0.001821, 0.01538] does not exclude 0
evidence: payoff_var / monthly 2003–2025 / mean: 0.007642 [-8.458e-04, 0.01613] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 1.76, p = 0.0776; payoff_var / monthly 2003–2025 / mean: 0.007642 [-0.001821, 0.01538] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = 0.0788
caveat: Raw variance is dominated by a few crash months; quote it next to the scaled payoff.

claim: The VIX has exceeded the volatility that followed by 3.676 vol points on average (95% CI 2.578 to 4.774).
evidence: vol_spread_pts / monthly 2003–2025 / mean: 3.676 [2.578, 4.774] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC t, t = 6.56, p = 5.3e-11; vol_spread_pts / monthly 2003–2025 / mean: 3.676 [2.515, 4.742] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = ≤ 0.0001

claim: The typical (median) month pays the seller 48.0% of implied variance (95% CI 41.1% to 52.4%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / median: 0.4804 [0.4114, 0.5239] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), sign test (218/267 positive), p = 1.3e-26

claim: The variance seller wins in 81.6% of months (95% CI 76.6% to 85.8%), far more often than a coin flip.
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / win_rate: 0.8165 [0.7657, 0.8583] (Wilson (i.i.d.)), exact binomial (218/267), p = 1.3e-26; payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / win_rate: 0.8165 [0.764, 0.8652] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = ≤ 0.0001

claim: The scaled payoff is strongly negatively skewed (skewness -4.457, 95% CI -5.751 to -3.372): many small gains, a few huge losses.
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / skewness: -4.457 [-5.751, -3.372] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), D'Agostino skewness test (i.i.d.), p = 9.8e-43

claim: The raw variance payoff is negatively skewed (skewness -6.333, 95% CI -10.7 to 0.2349).
evidence: payoff_var / monthly 2003–2025 / skewness: -6.333 [-10.7, 0.2349] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), D'Agostino skewness test (i.i.d.), p = 1.1e-55
fallback: Say: the raw variance payoff has a large negative sample skewness, but it is driven by a few months (the block-bootstrap CI reaches zero), so lead with the scaled payoff's skewness instead.

claim: The payoff has fat tails: excess kurtosis 24.18 (95% CI 12.35 to 44.09; normal = 0).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / excess_kurtosis: 24.18 [12.35, 44.09] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), Anscombe–Glynn kurtosis test (i.i.d.), p = 4.3e-21

claim: The mean sits well below the median (mean − median = -23.8%, 95% CI -34.6% to -13.8%): a long left tail of bad months pulls the average down.
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / mean_minus_median: -0.2381 [-0.3462, -0.1377] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap (H0: mean = median), p = ≤ 0.0001

claim: Extreme losing months are far more common than a bell curve predicts: 10 months fall more than 3 standard deviations below the mean (95% CI 5.465 to 18.04).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / months_below_mean_minus_3sd: 10 [5.465, 18.04] (Wilson (i.i.d.), in months), exact binomial vs normal tail probability, p = 6.3e-12

claim: The average losing month is larger than the average winning month (|avg loss| / avg gain = 1.883, 95% CI 0.9759 to 2.931).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / loss_to_gain_ratio: 1.883 [0.9759, 2.931] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap (H0: |avg loss| = avg gain), p = 0.073
fallback: Say: the *worst* months are many times the average gain (descriptive facts below), but the *average* loss is not significantly bigger than the average gain. The lopsidedness is in the extreme tail, not the typical loss.

claim: Seller payoffs move with the S&P 500 over the same 21 days (correlation 0.5862, 95% CI 0.5014 to 0.6598): the seller loses when stocks fall.
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / corr_with_spx_fwd21_ret: 0.5862 [0.5014, 0.6598] (Fisher z (i.i.d.)), Pearson, p = 5.0e-26; payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / corr_with_spx_fwd21_ret: 0.5862 [0.4497, 0.6837] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), bootstrap, p = ≤ 0.0001
caveat: Same-window outcomes: this describes when losses happen, it is not a forecast made at t.

claim: In sell-off months (S&P down more than 5% over the window) the seller loses on average: mean scaled payoff -119.5% (95% CI -198.0% to -41.1%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / mean_in_selloff: -1.195 [-1.98, -0.4105] (t (i.i.d.)), one-sample t, t = -3.14, p = 0.00434
caveat: Conditioning on an outcome: descriptive, not forecastable at t.

claim: Sell-off months pay the seller 159.3% of implied variance less than other months (95% CI of the gap 85.6% to 236.5%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / diff_mean_selloff_minus_other: -1.593 [-2.365, -0.8562] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), Welch t, t = -4.16, p = 0.000317

claim: The worst 10% of S&P months (decile 1) carry 83.3% of all variance-seller losses (95% CI 45.2% to 94.5%); with no clustering they would carry about 10%.
evidence: payoff_var / monthly 2003–2025 / loss_share_in_decile_1: 0.8331 [0.4518, 0.945] (block bootstrap (6-month blocks)), permutation (10,000 shuffles; null mean 0.096), p = ≤ 0.0001

claim: It is the direction of the market, not just big moves: the worst S&P decile pays the seller 174.5% of implied variance less than the best decile (decile 10), although both contain large moves (95% CI of the gap 103.2% to 249.9%).
evidence: payoff_scaled / monthly 2003–2025 / diff_mean_decile_1_minus_decile_10: -1.745 [-2.499, -1.032] (bootstrap over the 2 deciles' months), Welch t, t = -4.56, p = 0.000113

claim: The VIX is a biased forecast of realised variance: an unbiased forecast (RV = 0 + 1·IV) is rejected (HAC Wald χ² = 2.717).
evidence: variance / monthly 2003–2025 / joint_a0_b1: 2.717, HAC Wald χ²(2) (H0: unbiased forecast, a = 0 and b = 1), p = 0.26; vol_pct / monthly 2003–2025 / joint_a0_b1: 75.06, HAC Wald χ²(2) (H0: unbiased forecast, a = 0 and b = 1), p = 5.0e-17; log_variance / monthly 2003–2025 / joint_a0_b1: 174.9, HAC Wald χ²(2) (H0: unbiased forecast, a = 0 and b = 1), p = 1.1e-38

claim: In log terms the VIX's bias is a constant over-statement: intercept -0.4919 (95% CI -1.04 to 0.0561) with a slope not significantly different from 1.
evidence: log_variance / monthly 2003–2025 / intercept_a: -0.4919 [-1.04, 0.0561] (Newey–West (6 lags)), HAC z (H0: a = 0), p = 0.0785
caveat: 'Slope not different from 1' is absence of evidence, not proof that b = 1.
fallback: Say: in logs the point estimate suggests a constant proportional over-statement, but it does not survive the multiple-testing correction. Use the joint unbiasedness rejection instead.
